sentences.text: Quetzalcoatlus was a member of the Azhdarchidae family, characterized by being toothless pterosaurs with rigid and unusually long necks.
Quetzalcoatlus northropi was among the largest azhdarchids, rivalled in size by Arambourgiania, Hatzegopteryx, and possibly Cryodrakon.
Based on limb morphology and azhdarchid tracks from South Korea, Quetzalcoatlus was likely quadrupedal.
Azhdarchid wings had an aspect ratio of 8.1, similar to storks and birds of prey, indicating reliance on thermals and updrafts for soaring.
The first Quetzalcoatlus fossils were discovered in 1971 by Douglas A. Lawson during his Master's degree field work.
The type specimen of Quetzalcoatlus northropi was recovered in 1971 from the Javelina Formation in Texas and described in 1975 by Douglas Lawson.
Lawson announced the discovery in the journal Science in March 1975, featuring a size comparison with a large aircraft and a Pteranodon on the cover.
The genus name refers to the Aztec god Quetzalcōātl and the species name honors Jack Northrop.
Recent estimates based on azhdarchid proportions place the wingspan of Quetzalcoatlus at 10 to 11 meters.
Recent estimates of the wingspan of Quetzalcoatlus northropi hover around 10 to 11 meters.
Recent research suggests Quetzalcoatlus likely hunted small prey on the ground like storks and ground hornbills.
Historical interpretations of Quetzalcoatlus diet included scavenging and skim-feeding.
Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni is suggested to have fed on small aquatic invertebrates near alkaline lakes.
Pteranodon gigas is a synonym of Quetzalcoatlus.
Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni was described by Andres and Langston Jr. in 2021.
In 2019, all azhdarchid remains from the Dinosaur Park Formation were revised as distinct from Quetzalcoatlus and named the new genus Cryodrakon.
A 2025 study found a Wyoming neck vertebra to be anatomically compatible with Q. lawsoni but forming a polytomy with Q. lawsoni, Q. northropi, and a Moroccan specimen in phylogenetic analysis.
Quetzalcoatlus lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Quetzalcoatlus lived in North America during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous.
Specimens from across Late Cretaceous North America were historically assigned to Quetzalcoatlus.
It is debated whether Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni should be placed within the genus Quetzalcoatlus.
In 2025, it was suggested that Quetzalcoatlus is polyphyletic and that Q. lawsoni is not the sister species to Q. northropi.
A study debated the classical interpretation of Quetzalcoatlus as the last of a dying lineage, suggesting many lineages persisted into the Late Cretaceous.
It cannot be determined whether indeterminate azhdarchid remains from Big Bend represent separate animals from Quetzalcoatlus.
